body:
What makes an energy transition just?

An energy transition is a change in how energy is produced, delivered and consumed. A transition towards lower-emission energy may involve greater use of renewable sources, improved efficiency, cleaner industrial processes and changes in transport and fuel use.

Such changes can produce environmental and economic benefits, but their effects are not shared equally. Some industries gain investment and employment, while others may lose demand. A region dependent on an older industry may suffer even if employment increases elsewhere.

A just energy transition seeks to make changes in the energy system environmentally sustainable while protecting affected people, promoting decent work, reducing inequality and sharing opportunities and burdens fairly.

The International Labour Organization's approach emphasises decent work, social protection, skills development and social dialogue. A just transition does not require preserving every existing job indefinitely. It requires planning for those whose livelihoods may be disrupted and enabling them to participate in new opportunities.

Who is affected?

Affected groupPossible difficultyRelevant response
WorkersLoss of employment, income or established occupational skills.Retraining, job placement and income protection.
RegionsDecline in local business activity or public revenue when a major industry contracts.Economic diversification and investment in alternative livelihoods.
ConsumersHigher energy prices or unequal access to new technologies.Targeted support, efficiency measures and consumer protection.
Local communitiesLand-use changes, displacement or unequal sharing of project benefits.Meaningful consultation and appropriate safeguards.

Workers and the geographical problem

Consider a region where coal mining supports not only mine workers but also transporters, repair workshops, small shops and local services. If coal demand falls, these activities may also be affected. At the same time, new solar or wind projects may create employment in different districts or states.

This creates a geographical mismatch: jobs may be created, but not in the places where jobs are lost. There may also be a skills mismatch: workers experienced in one industry may not immediately possess the qualifications needed in another.

Training is therefore most useful when it is connected to realistic employment opportunities. It may need to be combined with job matching, travel or relocation support, education and local industrial development. Training alone does not guarantee employment.

Social dialogue and public participation

Social dialogue involves consultation, negotiation and the exchange of information among governments, employers and workers or their representatives. Its purpose is to help shape policies and workplace changes rather than announce decisions after they have already been finalised.

Engagement with affected residents is also important. For example, the concerns of farmers and village communities affected by the siting of an energy project may differ from those of employees in an existing industrial plant. Both require attention, but they are not the same group.

Benefits and burdens are not automatically balanced

An increase in renewable-energy employment at the national level does not prove that every displaced worker has found a suitable new job. Similarly, a lower average cost of electricity does not establish that all households can afford it. A just transition therefore examines who benefits, who bears the cost, where the effects occur and when support is needed.

Prelims focus

  • A just transition combines environmental sustainability with social and economic fairness.
  • The ILO's just-transition framework emphasises decent work, social protection, skills and social dialogue.
  • Social dialogue primarily involves governments, employers and workers or their representatives.
  • Employment effects must be assessed across both industries and geographical regions.
  • Trap: Creating new jobs nationally does not automatically compensate workers who lose jobs in another region.

[International Labour Organization, Guidelines for a Just Transition towards Environmentally Sustainable Economies and Societies for All, adopted 2015 and published 2 February 2016; International Labour Organization, The MNE Declaration and a Just Transition, 12 December 2024; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter 7, Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues, section 7.5, printed pp. 122–124.]

title: Just Energy Transition: Fairness for Workers, Regions and Consumers

body:
Why existing energy investments may lose value

Energy infrastructure often requires substantial investment and is expected to operate for many years. Examples include power stations, mines, fuel pipelines, processing facilities and associated transport infrastructure. Owners generally expect these assets to generate income or provide services over their planned economic lives.

However, changes in technology, fuel demand, environmental regulation, operating costs or public policy can reduce the future usefulness or profitability of an investment.

A stranded asset is an asset that loses economic value or becomes unable to earn its expected return earlier than anticipated because circumstances have changed.

For example, a relatively new fuel-dependent facility may become uncompetitive if demand for its output falls sharply or a less costly alternative becomes widely available. It may still be physically capable of operating, yet its expected future income may no longer justify its original valuation.

Economic stranding is not the same as physical destruction. An asset may become financially unattractive while remaining technically usable. Equally, an old facility reaching the end of its planned service life is not necessarily an example of premature stranding.

What can cause energy assets to become stranded?

  • Technological change: A competing technology offers the same service at a lower cost or with better performance.
  • Market change: Demand for a particular fuel or service declines.
  • Policy change: New environmental requirements or other rules alter the economics of an investment.
  • Resource or operating constraints: A facility becomes more costly to operate because suitable inputs are difficult to obtain.

These are possible causes, not proof that every fossil-fuel facility will become stranded. The result depends on the asset's costs, contracts, remaining life and actual market conditions.

How losses can spread beyond the asset owner

The financial consequences of an underused facility may extend beyond the company that owns it. Lenders can face repayment problems. Workers and suppliers may lose income. Local governments may collect less revenue. If contracts or public guarantees require continued payments, some costs may fall on electricity purchasers or taxpayers.

This is why stranded-asset risk is relevant to both energy finance and just transition planning. A poorly managed transition can produce financial losses and regional hardship, even where the new energy system delivers long-term benefits.

Skills, social protection and regional investment

Transition assistance should respond to the actual source of hardship. Skills development helps workers qualify for new occupations. Social protection helps people maintain basic income or access essential services during unemployment or other disruptions. Regional economic diversification develops alternative sources of employment and revenue so that a locality is less dependent on one industry.

These measures are complementary. Retraining cannot replace temporary income support for a worker who has lost wages, and temporary payments cannot by themselves create a lasting local employment base.

Who finances the adjustment?

Possible financing sources include public expenditure, employer-funded programmes, private investment and appropriately designed development finance. Public funds may support training, essential services or local infrastructure. Private investment may create new enterprises and employment. The division of costs depends on policy choices, contractual obligations and available resources.

Government assistance has an opportunity cost: money spent on one programme is unavailable for other purposes unless additional resources are raised. Fairness therefore also requires examining how transition support is financed and whether assistance reaches those most affected.

Prelims focus

  • Stranded assets lose expected economic value earlier than anticipated.
  • Technological, market and policy changes can create stranding risk.
  • Asset stranding can affect lenders, workers, suppliers, communities and public finances.
  • Skills development, social protection and regional diversification address different problems.
  • Trap: A physically functioning asset can still be economically stranded.

[International Energy Agency, Portugal 2026, Executive Summary, discussion of declining gas-network use and stranded assets, consulted 16 November 2026; International Labour Organization, The Role of Active Labour Market Policies for a Just Transition, 29 June 2023; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development, printed pp. 166–170; International Energy Agency, Scaling Up Private Finance for Clean Energy in Emerging and Developing Economies, Executive Summary, 2023.]

pictures.alt: Lower expected income from an energy asset spreads risks to its owner, lenders, workers, suppliers, local government and, conditionally, consumers or taxpayers.
pictures.caption: Economic losses from an underused energy asset can affect several groups.

title: Stranded Assets, Skills and the Distribution of Transition Costs

body:
What is an electricity tariff?

An electricity tariff is the schedule of charges applicable to the supply or use of electricity under the relevant regulatory and contractual arrangements. The electricity bill paid by a consumer may include several components rather than one uniform price.

In a common retail tariff structure, a consumer pays a fixed charge associated with the connection or applicable billing category and an energy charge related to electricity consumed. Other adjustments, duties or authorised charges may also apply. The precise structure differs across consumer categories and tariff orders.

Electricity consumption is commonly measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh). A kilowatt-hour is a unit of electrical energy, whereas a kilowatt (kW) measures power. An energy charge expressed in rupees per kWh is therefore different from a charge associated with connected load or demand.

Illustrative electricity bill

Suppose a hypothetical tariff has a fixed charge of ₹100 and a uniform energy charge of ₹4 per kWh. For consumption of 100 kWh, the energy charge is ₹400 and the total before other charges is ₹500. This is only an example of the calculation; it is not an actual Gujarat tariff.

Who determines electricity tariffs in India?

The Electricity Act, 2003 provides the principal statutory framework. Electricity Regulatory Commissions perform tariff-related functions under the Act.

  • Section 61: Provides principles guiding tariff regulations, including commercial operation, efficiency, consumer interests, reasonable cost recovery and progressive reduction of cross-subsidies.
  • Section 62: Provides for determination of tariffs for generation supplied to distribution licensees, transmission, wheeling and retail sale of electricity by the appropriate regulatory commission.
  • Section 63: Provides for adoption of a tariff determined through a transparent bidding process conducted according to Central Government guidelines.
  • Section 65: Governs a subsidy required by a State Government for a consumer or class of consumers. The State Government must pay compensation in advance to the person affected by the subsidy, in the manner directed by the State Commission, for the subsidy direction to operate.

Tariff determination under Section 62 and tariff adoption under Section 63 are distinct statutory routes. A tariff emerging from an eligible competitive bidding process is not automatically the same as a cost-based retail tariff determined by the regulator.

Subsidy and cross-subsidy are different

An electricity subsidy reduces the amount borne by an eligible consumer through financial support, typically from the government under an applicable scheme.

Cross-subsidy occurs when one category of consumers pays charges above the cost attributable to its supply, helping support another category charged below its attributable cost.

FeatureGovernment subsidyCross-subsidy
Main source of supportGovernment fundsPayments collected from other consumer categories
PurposeReduce charges for specified eligible consumersSupport lower charges for one group through higher recovery from another
Important considerationBudgetary cost and timely paymentEffect on prices and fairness across consumer categories

For example, a State Government may support specified agricultural consumers through a subsidy. Separately, a tariff structure may require an industrial or commercial category to contribute more than its attributable supply cost, thereby supporting lower tariffs for another category. Both may influence affordability, but their funding arrangements are different.

Why tariff policy involves a balance

Electricity charges must address several objectives. If prices are too high for vulnerable households, access to essential energy services may be reduced. If the revenue available to the distribution utility is persistently inadequate and the gap is not funded, its ability to purchase electricity, maintain infrastructure and invest in reliable service may be weakened.

Tariff policy therefore connects affordability with financial sustainability. Targeted support can protect vulnerable consumers, while transparent cost recovery and efficient utility operations help maintain the supply system.

Gujarat's regulatory example

The Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission (GERC) determines regulated electricity tariffs within its jurisdiction. Its tariff orders distinguish among relevant distribution licensees and consumer categories.

For example, GERC issued a tariff order for Dakshin Gujarat Vij Company Limited (DGVCL) on 25 March 2026, covering tariff determination for FY 2026–27. The order stated that the revised retail tariffs would apply to electricity consumption from 1 April 2026. These dates describe that particular regulatory order, not a permanently fixed tariff rate.

Prelims focus

  • Section 61 of the Electricity Act, 2003 sets guiding principles for tariff regulations.
  • Section 62 concerns tariff determination; Section 63 concerns tariff adoption through qualifying competitive bidding.
  • Section 65 governs State Government tariff subsidies and the associated advance-payment requirement.
  • Government subsidy and consumer-category cross-subsidy have different funding sources.
  • GERC issued DGVCL's FY 2026–27 tariff order on 25 March 2026, with revised rates applicable from 1 April 2026.
  • Trap: A cross-subsidy is not necessarily paid from the government budget.

[Electricity Act, 2003, Sections 45 and 61–65, India Code, consulted 16 November 2026; Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission, DGVCL Tariff Order, Case No. 2581 of 2025, dated 25 March 2026, Commission's Order, p. 153 and accompanying tariff schedule; GERC, Tariff Orders, FY 2026–27 entries, consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Government subsidies and cross-subsidies have different sources of financial support.
